leads.name: City of Monterey's 13 Local Landmark Trees
leads.why: Monterey Municipal Code Chapter 37-12 designates 13 individual trees as Local Landmark Trees, 'of such unusual size, prominence or health as to be of significant value to the community'. STILL UNRETRIEVED after a second, more thorough pass (2026-09-27). Tried and failed: monterey.municipal.codes/Code/37-12 and the monterey.gov ordinance page (both 403 to curl and WebFetch); library.municode.com's own JS app directly (curl and WebFetch both return only the static Angular shell, no server-rendered content, even with a Googlebot user-agent -- this site cannot be read without executing its JS, which no tool here can do); Wayback Machine (no snapshot exists for either the .codes mirror or the municode.com nodeId URL, confirmed via the CDX API, zero results); the city's own tree/parks pages (tree_ordinance_facts.php and the urban-forestry index both confirm '13 trees' but explicitly say 'Photos of Landmark Trees posted soon', i.e. no gallery or list is live); the haveyoursaymonterey.org Tree Ordinance Update engagement site (2025-2026, town halls Oct 2025, council study session March 2026, council action April 2026 -- links only back to the same Code/37-12 page, no exhibit); monterey.legistar.com search (found only an unrelated Monterey COUNTY case about landmark pines #442/#411 near a private residence, nothing about the city's 13); Monterey County Now / Monterey Herald coverage of the ordinance update (one article on residents wanting more flexibility names only generic 'oak trees' and a 'pine tree' on private property, no landmark-tree specifics); a substack post titled 'Holy Oak' by a local Monterey history writer (montereyneighborsandfriends.substack.com/p/holy-oak, 403 to both curl with browser UA and WebFetch -- unconfirmed whether it is even about a landmark tree, worth a browser-session retry). This remains the single highest-value lead for growing past the floor, but it may need a phone call to city staff (831-646-3860 / forestry@monterey.gov, city has offered this contact repeatedly in search results) or a public-records request rather than another web pass; the source is genuinely gated behind a JS-only municode viewer with no crawlable fallback and no archived copy anywhere.

blocked.name: The Vizcaino-Serra Oak (Junipero Oak)
blocked.why: Dead. Declared dead in 1904 and cut down in 1905; the preserved trunk was displayed at the Cathedral of San Carlos Borromeo for most of the 20th century and has since been removed. Hard rule: never doen aan dode bomen. Its site (Mission San Carlos / Monterey State Historic Park) could be mentioned in prose as history but is not a collectible entry.

blocked.name: The Ghost Tree(s) of Pescadero Point
blocked.why: Confirmed dead as a feature, not merely a worried lead. Wikipedia's own 'Ghost Trees' article, fetched directly (not a search summary), states plainly: 'the bleached trunks of dead cypress at the end of 17-Mile Drive.' Multiple other sources (Atlas Obscura's description, an SFGate headline 'California's most photographed tree should be allowed to die', a Roadtrippers/travel summary noting foresters expect the few living cypresses left there to die of cypress canker within 20 years) converge on the same picture: this is a cluster of predominantly dead, bone-bleached cypress trunks named collectively 'Ghost Trees' (plural), not one living, identifiable tree. Fails the alive test outright, and even setting that aside it is not one collectible point (no single named surviving specimen distinguished from the rest). Atlas Obscura, SFGate and pebblebeach.com's own tour page all returned 403 to WebFetch on this pass, so this rests on the Wikipedia fetch plus converging search summaries rather than every source being independently fetched; a future pass with browser access could firm this up further, but nothing found points the other way.

blocked.name: Crocker Grove's oldest Monterey cypresses
blocked.why: 17-Mile Drive stop 11, named after Charles Crocker; TripAdvisor and voicemap.me call it home to some of the oldest Monterey cypress specimens in the world, 'nearly 300 years old' per one WebSearch summary (not independently fetched, so treat that figure as a lead only). It is a GROVE though, not a single collectible point; would need a specific named/marked individual specimen within it to qualify, which was not found this pass.
